verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that Fāṭir, derived from fiṭr, figuratively describes God as cleaving through nothingness and bringing the heavens and earth into being for the first time. It resembles badīʿ and mubdiʿ, but ibdāʿ emphasizes creating without a prior model, whereas fiṭr emphasizes dispelling nonexistence and originating a thing. “The heavens and the earth” may denote the whole visible universe and all it contains by mention of its greatest parts, or specifically these two immense and wondrous creations. As a divine attribute, fātir al-samawāti wa al-arḍ denotes not merely a past act but uninterrupted creation: God continually bestows existence, and things would cease if this ceased.

The sequence “originator” and “maker” establishes why praise belongs exclusively to God: He originated the heavens and earth and made the angels winged messengers; thus He is exalted and praised, for He creates only beauty. Angels are created intermediaries between God and the visible world, entrusted with the affairs of creation and legislation (ʿālam al-takwīniyyah wa al-tashrīʿiyyah). They are honored worshippers who do not disobey Him. Since “the angels” occurs as a definite plural, the verse indicates—and proves—that all angels are messengers between God and creation in these two domains, not only those who descend to prophets. The Qur’an also calls the angels who take souls, record plots, and came to Abraham “messengers.”

Ajniḥah means wings, which in birds serve in place of hands and enable movement through the air. The angels possess what functions like wings, enabling them by God’s command to travel from heaven to earth, return, and move between places. The Qur’anic term does not require feathers or down, just as such terms as throne (ʿarsh), seat (kursī), tablet (lawḥ), and pen (qalam) do not require the corresponding familiar physical forms. “Two, three, and four” signifies repeated numbers: some angels have two pairs of wings, some three, and some four. “He adds to creation as He wills” further implies angels having more than four pairs. The closing declaration that Allah has power over all things most clearly explains all that precedes it.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s mercy here means blessing or sustenance (rizq): no one can prevent a blessing that God grants, nor provide one that God has withheld. “Open” means “send,” as its parallel with “send” in the second clause shows; it evokes divine mercy as treasures or coffers encompassing humankind, accessible only when God opens them. Sustenance is called a blessing arising from mercy to show that blessings emanate from God’s sheer mercy, not from self-interest or a need for self-exaltation.

“Thereafter” (min baʿdihi) indicates that God is first both in withholding and in giving. His might means that none can overcome His giving or withholding, and His wisdom means that both occur wisely and for what is best. Thus God alone gives and withholds, and does so with wisdom.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as a proof of the oneness (tawḥīd) of God in lordship (rubūbiyyah), addressed to idolaters and those who ascribe partners to Him. A being can be worshipped as a god only if it possesses lordship, including administration of creatures through the blessings by which they subsist. God alone created those blessings and the system that dispenses them; creation remains dependent on that administration. He alone is therefore their Lord and God.

“Remember” (udhkurū) means not to forget God’s blessing, rather than to perform a verbal act of dhikr. Sustenance (rizq), which prolongs existence, comes from heaven and earth, including such things as sunlight, rainfall, vegetation, and animal life. The verse deliberately asks whether there is another creator rather than another sustainer. This blocks the claim that, although God created the world, He appointed lesser gods to administer sustenance: sustainer here entails the creator of sustenance, and no other such creator exists.

“There is no god but He” glorifies God and declares that only the One who truly bestows blessings and sustenance is worthy of worship. “So how are you deluded?” consequently reproaches those who acknowledge this but turn from truth and monotheism to falsehood and polytheism. Grammatically, min is extraneous (zāʾidah) for generality; ghayr Allāh qualifies both “creator” and “provides for you”; an existence-predicate after “creator” is elided; and “There is no god but He” is an interjection before the concluding reprimand.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan consoles the Prophet: if people deny him despite the clear proofs, he should not grieve, since earlier messengers were likewise called liars by their peoples. All matters return to God, who will requite deniers as they deserve after the truth has appeared, and their denial cannot harm the Prophet.

The wording substitutes the statement that earlier messengers were denied for the implied instruction not to grieve, producing an inversion in which it structurally appears as the cause of grief. “And to Allah do all matters return” is joined to the statement about those earlier messengers.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan says that God’s true promise is the certain coming resurrection from the graves and recompense for good and evil deeds. Its outcome is severe punishment for those who belie the truth, and forgiveness and a great reward for believers who do righteous deeds.

The prohibition against being deceived by worldly life is addressed in reality to people: they must not be absorbed in its adornments and pleasures until the Day of Reckoning is forgotten and they turn from the truth. Archdeceiver (gharūr), an intensified term for one or something habitually excessive in deception, apparently refers to Satan, as the following verse reinforces. He deceives people about God by directing them to divine forbearance and clemency while turning them from His trials and His allowing them to decline gradually through their own conduct. They then imagine that heedlessness, sin, and rejection of truth have no consequence, and that worldly ease, power, and status constitute honor; Satan leads them to dismiss the promised reward and punishment, resurrection, reckoning, Garden, and Fire as superstition. Thus his deception concerns God’s treatment of human heedlessness and wrongdoing.

Perhaps archdeceiver may instead refer to the enticing glitter of the world itself, in which case the final prohibition reiterates and emphasizes the preceding one.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that Satan must be treated as an enemy because his sole aim is to seduce people away from a happy life in this world and the next. Taking him as an enemy means avoiding those who answer his call to falsehood and disobedience, which he implants through whispering and enticement.

His party (ḥizbahu) is the group united upon one aim. The explanatory lām in li-yakūnū shows that the ultimate purpose of Satan’s call is that his party become inhabitants of saʿīr, the raging fire, a Qur’anic name for Hell.
verses.7: Al-Mizan identifies this as the true divine promise: rejecters of truth face severe punishment, while believers who work righteous deeds receive forgiveness and a great reward. The indefinite forms of punishment, forgiveness, and reward leave their particular kinds unspecified; especially in punishment, this indicates differing degrees corresponding to differing degrees of denial and corruption.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan affirms the division between deniers, who face severe punishment, and believing righteous people, who receive forgiveness and a great reward: because the two are not alike, neither are their ends in the hereafter. The opening question has an elided conclusion, namely that one whose evil deeds are made fair to him is not like one who sees evil as evil. Its fāʾ makes it a consequence of the preceding division, and its intended subject is the denier (kāfir), who mistakes evil for beauty.

God’s leading astray whomever He wills and guiding whomever He wills explains this difference: He leads astray the denier who sees foul as fair and guides the righteous believer who sees foul as foul. This misguidance is not initial; it comes as a consequence of the denier’s conduct and outlook, so attributing it to God entails no injustice. The two groups reach different ends both because God promises punishment or mercy in accordance with guidance or misguidance, and because their guidance or misguidance accords with their contrary ways of seeing evil and good.

The Prophet is therefore told not to destroy himself through sorrow over their unbelief and denial. “In regret” (ḥasarātin) gives the reason for his soul’s chasing after them: grief over what has eluded him. God has led them astray because of their denial and their treating evil as good; He knows what they have done, and will judge and recompense them justly. It is thus unfitting for the Messenger to afflict himself over those who have strayed and earned punishment.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s sending of the winds, their stirring and spreading of the clouds, and the driving of those clouds to barren land concern rainfall and the ensuing growth of herbage. Unlike the similar verse in Sūrah al-Rūm, which focuses on people’s joy at rain, this verse focuses on the earth’s becoming verdant. Though phrased in the present tense, both verses recount what has already occurred; ithārah denotes the spreading or stirring up of something.

The dead land is land without vegetation, and giving it life means causing herbage to grow where it had not grown before. This may refer literally to plants or, metaphorically, to such things as food, nourishment, growth, and birth. Its likeness to the resurrection lies in God’s restoring life to dead human beings and raising them from their graves, just as He restores vegetation after it has shrivelled.

The shift from the third person in Allah sends the winds to the first person in We drive them perhaps indicates that the winds are initially sent by an unseen agent before the clouds appear as evidence of that sending; once the clouds appear, the pronoun changes to We, expressing divine greatness. The wording needs no further pronoun after aḥyaynā or repetition of “land,” since the stated context makes the referent clear.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains ʿizzah as the quality that prevents one from being overcome: originally firmness or hardness, then the invincibility, dominance, superiority, rarity, difficulty, pride, or disdain conveyed by related usages. In its true sense, only Allah is ʿazīz, for every other being is essentially poor, dependent, and without real ownership even of itself, except insofar as God mercifully grants it a share of His ʿizzah, as with the believers. Thus, whoever seeks glory must seek it from Allah through worship, which yields faith and righteous deeds.

The goodly word is not mere utterance but a true, soul-uplifting meaning: the beliefs upon which deeds rest, foremost the word of tawḥīd from which true beliefs arise. Its ascent means its nearness to God—and, when embodied in a believer, the believer’s nearness to Him—while divine acceptance is a necessary consequence of that ascent. True belief necessarily appears in deeds concordant with it; repeated action further establishes and manifests the underlying belief. A righteous deed is noble and accepted only when marked by servitude and sincerity and befitting true belief. It therefore raises the goodly word toward God: the righteous deed is the subject of yarfaʿuhu and the goodly word its object.

The commentary judges unlikely other explanations: that ascent means only acceptance and reward; that angels carry records of faith and obedience upward, or merely ascend to heaven; that the goodly word raises the deed, making deeds beneficial only through tawḥīd; or that God raises the deeds. The initial interpretation is the most immediate one.

Those who plot evil schemes, especially polytheists seeking ʿizzah through their gods, receive severe punishment, and their specific plots perish rather than producing either happiness or glory. Although some exegetes connect this particularly with the Quraysh’s schemes at Dār al-Nadwah to seize, exile, or kill the Prophet, whose consequences were turned against them at Badr, Al-Mizan regards that as a good application while maintaining the verse’s generality. The verse contrasts their futile search for honor through other gods with the path by which belief in divine oneness ascends and righteous deeds raise it: one who approaches God receives honor from its source, whereas evil plotters neither ascend nor gain glory.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan states that the verse concerns humanity’s creation: remotely from dust and, at the later stage of individual generation, from a drop. Exegetes variously understand creation from dust as Adam’s creation, to which his descendants are appended; as referring to Adam alone; or as the literal creation of the human race, encompassing Adam’s creation from dust and the subsequent stages from a drop. The first understanding is figurative with respect to later humans, whereas the last is neither figurative nor confined to Adam. Each reading finds support in Qur’anic verses. Making humans into pairs means their creation as male and female; it has also been explained as their capacity to mate or their division into groups and tribes.

No female’s pregnancy or delivery occurs apart from God’s accompanying knowledge; bi-ʿilmihi attaches to both carrying and giving birth. The alternative that it merely describes the female subject conflicts with the apparent sense. Likewise, no lifespan is lengthened or shortened except as recorded in a book. The construction indicates that a person can reach old age only after a long lifespan has been decreed, and that shortening refers to the lifespan of one for whom length is initially decreed.

The book is the fixed and unalterable Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), in which the lengthening or shortening of each person’s life for its respective cause is inscribed. This differs from the Book of Erasing and Recording (kitab al-maḥw wa al-ithbāt), which may change; the verse concerns fixed, recorded knowledge. Other interpretations are weak. God’s precise governance of the origin and continuance of every species and each of its members is easy for Him because His knowledge and power encompass all things; He is the Lord of humanity and of everything else.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains the sweet sea as good, thirst-quenching, pleasant water, and the ujāj sea as water whose saltiness or bitterness burns. Fresh flesh denotes tender, wholesome meat—fish, or fish together with seabirds—and the ornaments are pearls, coral, and shells. Ships “plowing” the sea describes their prows cleaving the water, and their passage enables people to seek God’s bounty, namely sustenance, so that they may give thanks. The singular tarā addresses everyone capable of seeing, while the surrounding plural address concerns those who benefit from the sea. Laʿalla expresses an objective hope, not a hope attributed to God Himself.

The two seas have also been interpreted as a metaphor for believer and disbeliever. Though both share much in human endeavor and may share traits such as courage or generosity, the believer retains his original inner nature and reaches eternal happiness, whereas the disbeliever departs from that nature and is punished. Their shared benefits resemble the food and ornaments obtained from the two seas, while their essential difference resembles pure sweet water and water that has become salty. Some responses to the objection that pearls and coral occur only in salt water either take the verse to mean that the seas share benefits without every benefit occurring in each, or maintain that freshwater pearls are possible and that the objection is baseless.

The commentary also presents the literal reading as the stronger account: the verse enumerates divine blessings and the differing yet shared and distinctive benefits of fresh and salt water, thereby establishing God’s lordship. This is supported by the similarly literal description in Sūrah al-Naḥl: And He is the one who gave you mastery over the sea, so that you might eat fresh flesh from it and take from it ornaments that you wear. And you see the ships plowing through it so that you may seek His bounty, so that you might be grateful. (16:14) The claim that ornaments cannot be found in fresh water is rejected, since such ornaments are reported in both fresh and salt water.

Al-Mizan notes that (35:12) has fīhi mawākhir and li-tabtaghū without a preceding wa, whereas 16:14 has mawākhir fīhi and wa li-tabtaghū. Perhaps Sūrah al-Naḥl emphasizes taskhīr, God’s granting mastery over nature; delaying fīhi clarifies travel through the sea, and the conjunction leaves the purposes of that mastery unrestricted rather than limiting them to seeking bounty. Here the point is God’s provision and governance in answer to deniers of the Prophetic message, so seeking His bounty alone suffices. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī similarly reports that Sūrah al-Naḥl gives priority to the blessing of ships passing through water amid its discussion of numerous blessings, whereas the wording here suggests that this is not the primary point, whether it is a digression or the conclusion of the metaphor.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains God’s making night enter day and day enter night as the continuous seasonal alternation in which days and nights respectively lengthen and shorten. The present-tense yūlij conveys this perpetuity. By contrast, the sun and moon follow fixed courses for their appointed term, hence the distinct expression that God has put them into human service.

Since human creation and administration on land, sea, earth, and sky all return to God, He alone is the believers’ Lord: He truly owns them and governs their affairs. All dominion consequently belongs to Him. Those invoked besides Him—the idols and lords to whom people pray—possess not even a qiṭmīr, an expression for something insignificant, whether understood as the covering or remnant upon a date kernel, or as a tiny seed within it. The phrase therefore categorically denies that anything besides God owns creation.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse confirms the utter lack of ownership of those invoked besides Allah. Earthen idols neither hear nor perceive a caller. The lords associated with such idols, including angels and holy men, are occupied with their own duties and possess no independent faculty of hearing; they hear only if God makes them hear. If the statement that they would not respond concerns the idols, it means that they have no power to answer in word or deed. If it concerns their supposed lords, their power itself is from God, who will not permit them to answer one who invokes them as lords. As the verse says: The Messiah did not disdain being a servant of Allah, nor do the angels near [Him]. Whoever haughtily disdains to worship Allah shall [still] be gathered before Him. (4:172)

On the Day of Resurrection, those made partners with Allah will reject the worship directed to them, disassociate themselves from their worshippers, and not intercede for them. This is reiterated in: And who is more astray than the ones who call on ones other than Allah—ones who shall not respond to them until the Day of Resurrection, until which they will be have been heedless of their call. And when people are resurrected, they will be enemies to them and reject the way they were worshipped (46:6).

“No one informs you like the one who is aware” means that none can disclose the reality as does one who truly knows it. Although the preceding address is plural, this final statement addresses the Prophet directly, either because the prior audience failed to understand the truth or because the masses are addressed in the guise of a private address to him.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that the beliers’ worship of other gods implied that they considered themselves independent of God and God, exalted above this, somehow in need of them. The verse refutes this by assigning complete faqr to human beings and complete ghināʾ to God: as opposites, neediness and needlessness exclude one another. God is essentially independent and can dispense with or destroy them; they are essentially dependent and cannot become independent of Him through anything else.

This dependence follows from their being created and governed by God, while His independence follows from His being their Creator and Manager. His being praised likewise concerns His acts of creating and managing; the possibility that He may erase them and bring a new creation is among the manifestations of this praise.

Although the verse addresses human beings, this does not exclude the dependence of all other creatures, since the reason given is general. It is effectively an address to all created beings, who need their Creator and Manager. The commentary finds the proposed explanations for restricting faqr to humans—rhetorical emphasis, priority of the present audience, or a grammatical distinction between al-nās and al-fuqarāʾ—at odds with the verse’s import and context. The explanation that the restriction is relative rather than absolute may have some merit.

God is praised whether He gives or withholds. When He gives, He does not do so in exchange for something such as gratitude, for any apparent exchange was already decreed; and when He withholds, none may dispute with Him, since no one truly owns anything.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that God can obliterate people and replace them with a new creation without suffering any harm, for He has no need of either the old or new creation. The new creation would praise and glorify Him, yet He would remain independent of it. He is praised because He has made generosity incumbent upon Himself, and such replacement is not difficult for Him in His absolute power.

The assertion that this is not difficult confirms His needlessness, while bringing forth a new creation follows from His being ḥamīd. The meaning accords with: And your Lord is needless, the possessor of mercy. If He wishes, He could destroy you and replace you with whoever He wills (6:133).
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that God can obliterate people and replace them with a new creation without suffering any harm, for He has no need of either the old or new creation. The new creation would praise and glorify Him, yet He would remain independent of it. He is praised because He has made generosity incumbent upon Himself, and such replacement is not difficult for Him in His absolute power.

The assertion that this is not difficult confirms His needlessness, while bringing forth a new creation follows from His being ḥamīd. The meaning accords with: And your Lord is needless, the possessor of mercy. If He wishes, He could destroy you and replace you with whoever He wills (6:133).
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains wizr as the mountain-like burden of sin: no soul bears any portion of another’s sin, even that of a near relative, and each is accountable only for what it has earned. Thus, even if a heavily burdened person asks another to carry the slightest part of the burden, no one can do so.

The threatened destruction concerns the beliers, whose sealed hearts do not benefit from the divine call; it does not make believers bear the beliers’ burden. The two groups are unequal, like the blind and seeing, darkness and light, shade and heat, and life and death.

“You can only warn” means that warning benefits those who fear their Lord in secret and establish prayer, the foremost worship. It does not mean that these qualities must precede warning; rather, the warning produces their fear and observance, since otherwise the effect would be made a condition of its cause. “Whoever purifies himself” replaces fear and prayer with the intended result of the divine invitation: purification of the soul, adorned by hidden fear of God and prayer.

God gains nothing by calling people to purify themselves; their purification benefits themselves alone, confirming His independence and praise. Their return to Allah ensures that purification is not futile: both those who purify themselves and those who do not will be judged and recompensed, and the purified will receive the better recompense.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes these contrasts as continuing “And to Allah is the return”: they metaphorically distinguish those who purify themselves from those who belie the truth and show that their outcomes cannot be the same. Some exegetes instead connect them to “and the two seas are not alike” (35:12). The repeated lā intensifies the negation. Ḥarūr is said to mean intense sunlight, a hot wind, or a daytime hot wind whose heat persists by night.
verses.20: Al-Mizan takes these contrasts as continuing “And to Allah is the return”: they metaphorically distinguish those who purify themselves from those who belie the truth and show that their outcomes cannot be the same. verses.21: Al-Mizan takes these contrasts as continuing “And to Allah is the return”: they metaphorically distinguish those who purify themselves from those who belie the truth and show that their outcomes cannot be the same. Some exegetes instead connect them to “and the two seas are not alike” (35:12). The repeated lā intensifies the negation. Ḥarūr is said to mean intense sunlight, a hot wind, or a daytime hot wind whose heat persists by night.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains that the sequence from the blind and seeing through the living and dead consists of metaphors for believers and those who reject the truth, together with the consequences of their deeds. “Allah makes whoever He wishes hear” concerns the faithful whom God has enlivened and prepared inwardly to listen, as in: Or whoever was dead, and We enlivened him and made him a light… (6:122). The Prophet is only a means, while guidance belongs to God. “Those in the grave” are the dead, meaning the truth-rejecters whose hearts have been sealed and whom the Prophet cannot make hear.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet can do no more than warn: whether people are guided or go astray, and whether the misguided receive the recompense of their evil, lies with God. Though he is ordinarily described as both a bearer of glad tidings (bashīr) and a warner (nadhīr), only the latter is mentioned here because warning is the present subject.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet’s mission of glad tidings and warning is neither strange nor unprecedented: this is God’s established practice with His creation, and every earlier people had a warner pass through it. In context, nadhīr means a messenger appointed by God (rasūl mabʿūth min ʿind Allāh), not merely any prophet or knowledgeable preacher who warns. Nor must every people’s warner have belonged to that people, for the verse says a warner “passed through them” (khalā fihā), rather than being “from them” (khalā minhā).
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that earlier peoples likewise called their messengers liars, although the messengers brought bayyināt, the signs that testify to their truth; zubur, likely scrolls or scriptures celebrating God without ritual statutes; and kitābun munīr, a revealed book containing ritual law, such as the books of Noah and Abraham, the Torah of Moses, and the Gospel of Jesus.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s “seizing” those who rejected the truth is a metaphor for punishing them, and that nakīr means inkār: denial or disavowal.

The commentary further maintains, on intellectual and scriptural grounds, that no human nation was deprived of a warner bringing the true prophetic call. Yet a prophet need not have originated from the nation to which he warned, and there is no proof that he must have done so.

In principle, prophetic calls must reach every member of the societies to which prophets are sent. In material practice, however, intervening causes may prevent some persons from comprehending the call, just as universal natural capacities may fail to be realized in particular cases. Therefore, the necessity of warning every people does not require that every individual be guided directly or indirectly by a prophet. Whoever receives the call has had the proof completed against him; for one addressed by it but prevented from receiving it, the proof is not completed. Such persons are among the “weak,” whose destiny rests with God: Except for the weak—men, women, and children—who have no means and cannot find a way (4:98).
verses.27:
Al-Mizan presents the rain, the differently coloured fruits it brings forth, and the white, red, and intensely black mountain streaks as a proof of God’s oneness. Rain is the principal agent in the growth of fruit; if physical dependence on this one agent alone explained the result, fruits would be alike in colour. Nor do differing internal factors within species finally account for the diversity, since all are composed of the same physical matter; its ultimate source must be a metaphysical agent that governs things and directs them to different ends.

The stronger reading of “fruits of various colors” is actual variation of colour, corresponding to their differences of taste, fragrance, and other properties, rather than merely different kinds of fruit. The shift from third-person speech to “We bring forth” draws attention to God’s power and wisdom in bringing things anew into being; perhaps it also indicates that the matter lies directly between people and God, with no one to intercede, aid, or save them from punishment.

Judad, plural of juddah, means paths or roads; bīḍ and ḥumr are plurals of “white” and “red”; and gharābīb sūd denotes intense blackness, with sūd either reinforcing or specifying gharābīb. “Of various colors” apparently describes the mountain streaks themselves. These “paths” may be actual traversable roads or coloured streaks extending over mountain faces.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan says that mankind, land animals, and cattle, including camels, sheep, and cows, vary in colour as fruits and mountains do. Kadhalik most plausibly completes an implied statement concerning all the preceding varieties; the alternative that connects it to the fear of those who contemplate these signs is remote in both wording and meaning.

The verse resumes the argument by showing that reflection upon divine signs produces true faith and reverence in those who know, unlike the ignorant. It thus clarifies that the people effectively warned are those who truly fear their Lord. Al-ʿulamāʾ are those who know God through His names, attributes, and acts with a deep, complete knowledge that gives certainty, removes doubt and unrest, and appears in deeds that accord with words. Their fear is true reverence, accompanied by inward and outward humility.

God’s might means that He is ever victorious and cannot be overcome, so those who truly know Him revere Him in every respect. Because He is forgiving, repeatedly pardoning sins and slips, they believe in Him, draw near to Him, and desire to meet Him.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that reciting the book of Allah, or tilāwah, means reciting the Qur’an, an act God praises. Establishing prayer means performing it constantly without neglect. Spending secretly refers to voluntary, Sunnah-encouraged charity, concealed to avoid showing off and preserve sincerity; spending openly refers to obligatory contributions, such as zakāt and khums, and encourages others to give.

The imperishable exchange is one that is never destroyed. Exegetes differ whether “hoping for an exchange that will never perish” is the predicate of the sentence beginning with inna in this verse, or the predicate of “That He may pay them their rewards in full” in the following verse, explaining the purpose for which they perform these acts.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan takes the clause as the consequence of reciting the Book, maintaining prayer, and spending: those who do these deeds will receive their good reward completely. “Increase them in His bounty” may mean the multiplication of good deeds and their recompense, or it may mean something beyond multiplication of reward, such as the further gift available in heaven.

God does this because He is forgiving, pardoning their slips, and gracious (shakūr), rewarding them and bestowing further blessings from Himself.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that huwa reiterates the subject before the sentence proceeds. In huwa al-ḥaqq, the al- intensifies the assertion: the revealed Book is truth unmingled with falsehood, not the sole truth.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains inheritance as the transfer of something that its former possessor used and benefited from to others who will use it, pass it down through generations, and benefit from it; this applies to wealth, knowledge, position, and the Book. A group may inherit the Book even though only some uphold its requirements, as with the Israelites.

Here the Book is specifically the Qur’an, as the preceding verse identifies it as the Book revealed to the Prophet; the definite article does not mean the class of all revealed books. Al-iṣṭifāʾ means selecting the choicest and purest thing, unlike ikhtiyār, which is selecting the best from among many. Min in min ʿibādinā can be explanatory, indicate a range’s starting point, or select some from many, but it appears at first to be explanatory.

Exegetes have identified the chosen servants as the prophets, the Israelites, Muḥammad’s community, its scholars, or the Prophet’s descendants through Fāṭimah al-Zahrāʾ. The last view is reinforced by many well-sourced (mustafiḍah) narrations from Imām al-Bāqir and Imām al-Ṣādiq. They are included in the family of Abraham, know the Qur’an, and are inseparable from it, as stated in the highly transmitted (mutawātir), agreed-upon report: “I am leaving behind among you the two weighty things, the book of God and my descendants, the people of my house. They shall not separate until they are brought back to the fount [in Paradise].” On this reading, thumma conveys a delayed sequence: after revealing the Qur’an to the Prophet, God caused his offspring—whom He chose with the family of Abraham—to inherit it. The possessive in “Our servants” is then honorific.

“Among them” may refer to the chosen inheritors, who are divided into one who wrongs his soul, one who follows a middle course, and one foremost in good; the true inheritor who knows and preserves the Book is foremost. Alternatively, it may refer to all God’s servants: the chosen are only some servants, because not all—including wrongdoers, the moderate, and the foremost—are fit to receive this inheritance. Al-Mizan supports the first reading, since an entire group can inherit even if only some can truly bear the inheritance.

The division indicates that those who wrong themselves commit misdeeds, referring to Muslims who bear the Qur’an; the middle group occupy an intermediate position; and the foremost surpass both in nearness to God by His permission. The latter are the Imam, or others through God’s permission. The inheritance is a high grace from God, not an achievement earned by people.

Al-Mizan says this is what the context indicates and that narrations support it, while noting extensive disagreement. Thumma has been read as sequence in narration, rank, or time, and as attached either to “We revealed” or “which We revealed.” Inheritance has been taken literally or as God’s allocating it by judgment. The Book has been read as the Qur’an or all revealed books; min as partitive, initial, or explanatory; “servants” accordingly; “Our” as honorific or not; and “among them” as returning either to the chosen or to all servants. The three classes have also been interpreted respectively as one whose outward state exceeds his inward state, one whose two states are equal, and one whose inward exceeds his outward; as the Prophet’s companions, the following generation, and everyone after them; or as sinners immersed in misdeeds, the moderate, and those nearest God. Many further views exist.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains yuḥallawn as being ornamented or adorned, and asāwir as bracelets or sets of bracelets. The verse apparently elaborates the “high grace”: according to Majmaʿ al-Bayān, it explains that grace as gardens, the reward of gardens, or entry into gardens.
verses.34: Al-Mizan records the view that the sadness removed in heaven is the grief arising from worldly trials. It also records that it may be grief after death, or the lingering distress caused by misdeeds when people enter the eternal garden. The latter applies to those who wrong their souls or follow a middle course, not to those foremost in good, who have no evil deeds for which to suffer. This last interpretation best accords with their words, “Our Lord is forgiving, gracious.”
verses.35: Al-Mizan explains dār al-muqāmah as an abiding dwelling that its inhabitants neither leave nor see changed. Naṣab means hardship and exhaustion, while lughūb means helplessness and the exhaustion of seeking one’s livelihood. By God’s bounty, though they do not deserve it, the inhabitants of the Garden experience neither toil nor fatigue, nor helplessness or weariness in seeking what they desire, for there they have whatever they wish. “Out of His bounty” accords especially with the preceding description of this as a high grace.
verses.36: Al-Mizan says that the l- in lahum indicates that hellfire is the rejecters’ recompense and will not be separated from them. They do not die despite the severity of its punishment, but remain in it; nor is their punishment lightened. This is the recompense of the intensely ungrateful.
verses.37: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains yaṣṭarikhūn as a cry or appeal for help. The deniers of truth call for succor in the Fire and ask their Lord to remove them so that they may perform righteous deeds rather than their former evil deeds. They are answered that they were given a lifespan sufficient for anyone able to take heed to do so, and that a warner came to them, but they neither heeded nor believed. They are therefore told to taste the punishment: the unjust will have no one to save them.
verses.38: Al-Mizan concludes that, because Allah knows what is hidden in the heavens and earth and what lies in hearts, He will treat people and call them to account according to their inward beliefs and the effects of their deeds, whether or not their outward state matches their inward reality.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains khalāʾif as the plural of khalīfah, meaning that successive human generations inherit responsibility and authority to use and benefit from the earth as their predecessors did. This succession arises from the human faculty of generation, which divides humanity into past and future generations. Yet granting humans this earthly authority is itself a mode of governing creation, not a delegation that removes God's own lordship. Since the Creator of human beings is their Lord, and God is their Creator even according to His opponents, the verse proves the oneness of His lordship and excludes partners.

Disbelief in this truth, and the attribution of lordship to another, harms only the disbeliever. Kufr increases a person in divine hatred (maqt) and loss because human nature seeks perfection and increase: submission to God increases perfection and nearness, whereas denial increases divine displeasure and loss. Loss is the person's own natural consequence of exchanging faith and happiness for denial and misery; hatred is qualified as being “with their Lord” because it concerns God's perspective. Divine love and hate are attributes of act (ṣifāt al-afʿāl), external to the divine essence: love is God's spreading mercy over someone, while hate is His withholding and distancing that mercy.

The commentary then explains that the alleged partners are called “their” partners because the polytheists themselves claim them as partners to God. If these worshipped beings were lords, they would create and manage some part of the universe, since creation and management cannot be separated. Yet neither the visible world nor a revelation from God provides evidence that they created anything or share in the heavens. A revealed book affirming their lordship and authorizing their worship would be required, but none has been given; “Have We given them a book?” specifically denies a divinely bestowed book, and its pronouns refer to the polytheists, not to the alleged partners.

Perhaps the differing wording about earth and heavens reflects that “earth” here denotes the physical world and what is upon it, while “heavens” denotes the heavenly realms and what they contain: the question about creation of the earth also implies the denial of any share in it, for participation in lordship depends on creation. The polytheists therefore have no proof. They merely delude one another with promises of intercession and flattery, as predecessors and leaders deceive their followers. The argument applies generally to worship of idols, angels, jinn, saints, planetary and stellar spirits, other beings, and humans such as Jesus.

verses.41:
Al-Mizan notes a view that treats the verse as a new and independent refutation of partners, on the ground that a contingent thing requires conditions both for its coming-to-be and for its continued existence. What appears more fitting, however, is that the preceding proof of God's exclusive lordship is extended from human successorship to all creation, the heavens and the earth.

Bringing a thing into existence after nonexistence differs from making it endure in existence. Its continuance thus requires creational act after creational act; preserving and managing it are, in this respect, a continuous creation. The enduring order observable in creation shows this ongoing management. God alone, acknowledged even by opponents as Creator, is therefore the Creator and Administrator of the heavens and earth without a partner.

“Allah upholds” (yumsik) retains the basic sense of holding or grasping, though some exegetes render it as preventing or protecting. In either case, the expression is figurative for perpetuation: God continually bestows existence so that the universe does not undergo evanescence or destruction. The view that an tazūlā means that the heavens and earth remain distinct—so that neither sinks into or rises to the other—also appears sound.

In context, their “disappearance” most likely means waning away, since simultaneous upholding and disappearance would otherwise be incongruous: if they began to wane, no one but God could sustain them or bestow existence on them. It is also possible that disappearance is literal, in which case upholding means possessing the power to uphold them. God's being clement and forgiving means that, through forbearance, He does not hasten the final end, and through forgiveness He staves off their perishing until its appointed time. Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm likewise describes these names as indicating that He does not immediately punish people for their crimes but keeps the heavens and earth upheld and tranquil.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that jahd aymānihim means that they swore with utmost effort and exertion, while nufūr means aversion, distancing oneself, or fleeing. The verse concerns the Quraysh, who swore before the Prophet's appointment that, if a warner came to them, they would be more rightly guided than the other communities that had received warners, such as Jews and Christians. Their claim implicitly recognized that they had not previously received a warner; they asserted that, once they did, belief in him would make them surpass those earlier peoples in guidance. Yet when the Prophet came as the warner, his coming increased them only in flight and aversion.

A report in al-Durr al-Manthūr from Abū Hilāl and Ibn Jarīḥ relates that, after hearing that the People of the Book had denied their messengers, the Quraysh cursed the Jews and Christians and swore that, if a messenger came to them, they would be the most guided people. The context supports this account.

Some exegetes take “any of the other nations” generically, referring to every community that had denied its messenger, including Jews, Christians, and others. Another interpretation takes it to mean a uniquely designated people, “the one people,” distinguished from all others; Al-Mizan judges this latter reading imposed and farfetched.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan cites al-Rāghib's definition of makr as deceptive treatment of others to attain an end. Makr may be praiseworthy when it is a plan for good, but the makr in this verse is blameworthy, an evil scheme. “Arrogance in the land” and “evil plots” give the reasons for the people's aversion from the Prophet: they turn away in order to exalt themselves on earth and pursue evil plotting. Some instead connect “evil plot” directly to aversion through a genitive construction, but its sequel makes clear its effect.

An evil plot ultimately afflicts only its plotters. It may temporarily harm those at whom it is directed, but that effect passes, whereas its evil remains in the plotters' souls and appears upon them; they are justly requited for it in this world or the next. Majmaʿ al-Bayān likewise states that the recompense of such plotting falls only upon those who devised it. Thus the statement functions as a proverb, like the declarations that insolence and oath-breaking injure one's own soul.

The rhetorical question, “What are they waiting for,” follows from this principle: by plotting evil and belying God's signs, they await only the treatment given to earlier peoples—divine chastisement. God's sunnah admits neither change nor diversion. Tabdīl al-sunnah would be to exchange safety and blessing for punishment; taḥwīl al-sunnah would be to remove punishment from those who deserved it and place it upon those who did not. Neither occurs, because God's decrees are not subject to alternative opinions or exceptions. The verse was realized when God punished the plotting polytheists at Badr and many were killed. Its address may be to the Prophet specifically or to all who hear it.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan takes the fate of the earlier, more powerful nations as evidence that God's sunnah endures: despite their strength, God punished them when they plotted and denied the truth. The verse therefore intensifies the warning to the Meccan polytheists. They should fear God, believe, and cease plotting and denial, since the destruction of those former peoples shows the consequence of such conduct.

Nothing in the heavens or earth, including no plot or scheme, escapes God. As the Knowing, He is never unaware and cannot be deceived by their devices; as the Powerful, nothing can overcome Him.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that God's taking people to account here means worldly retribution for the accumulated sins of all people, not merely the plotters and deniers mentioned immediately before. If He exacted such an account, no creature would remain upon the face of the earth. “Its face” (ẓahrihā, literally “its back”) means the earth's surface. Dābah primarily means every human being who walks upon it, male or female, young or old; possibly it includes all creeping animals as well, whose destruction would follow the destruction of humankind, for they were created for human beings.

The commentary rejects the view that universal destruction would arise from the evil portents of sinners, because the consequences of sin should afflict the wrongdoers rather than others: “None shall bear the burden of another” (35:18). The warning that a distress may not seize only wrongdoers instead concerns a punishment that befalls wrongdoers specifically, not the whole mass of people.

God nevertheless grants people respite until an appointed term, understood as death or the resurrection. When it arrives, they will be requited for everything they did, for God sees His servants and knows their deeds; the statement that Allah sees His servants expresses the cause in place of its effect, namely their requital.

The verse answers an implicit question raised by the warning to the plotting polytheists and by God's irresistible power: if former deniers were destroyed, why are other people left to commit evil? The answer is that, although God could obliterate all people for their deeds, He decreed that they should dwell on earth and receive provision for a time, as in You have a place of rest on the earth and a livelihood, for a time (2:36). He therefore delays their accounting until death or resurrection, when He deals with them according to what they wrought.
